topics.title: BJT action
topics.essence: A forward-biased base–emitter junction injects electrons into a base much thinner than their diffusion length. Nearly all reach the reverse-biased collector and are swept across: I_C = I_S·e^(qV_BE/kT). Holes sent back to the emitter make I_B = I_C/β.
topics.check: Why does a thinner base, or a more heavily doped emitter, raise β?

topics.title: BJT regions
topics.essence: Forward active: base–emitter on, base–collector off, V_BE ≈ 0.7 V and I_C = βI_B. Saturation: both junctions on, V_CE ≈ 0.1 V and I_C < βI_B. Cut-off: neither on. A BJT's saturation is like a MOSFET's triode, not its saturation.
topics.check: A BJT with β = 100 gets I_B = 10 μA, but its collector circuit can pass at most 0.5 mA. Which region is it in, and roughly what is V_CE?

topics.title: Early effect
topics.essence: Raising V_CE widens the collector depletion region into the base and thins it, so I_C creeps up with V_CE. The output curves extrapolate back to −V_A on the voltage axis, and r_o = V_A/I_C.
topics.check: Lighter base doping lets the collector's depletion region eat further into the base. Does the Early voltage V_A go up or down?

topics.title: hybrid-π model
topics.essence: Around its bias point a BJT is a source g_m·v_π from collector to emitter, with g_m = I_C/(kT/q) and r_o across it. Unlike a MOSFET its base draws current: r_π = β/g_m from base to emitter, so source resistance divides the signal.
topics.check: A BJT with β = 100 is biased at 1 mA. What are g_m and r_π, and what happens to r_π if the bias current doubles?

links.why: The emitter junction is a forward-biased diode injecting minority carriers into the base.
A base far shorter than the diffusion length gives a straight-line profile, and almost no carriers recombine on the way.
Which of the two junctions is forward biased decides the region.
V_BE ≈ 0.7 V and V_CE,sat ≈ 0.1 V are diode on-voltages and their difference.
I_C is set by the base width, so anything that thins the base raises it.
The collector depletion region widens as √V and takes its width out of the base.
The same idea in the MOSFET: the effective length shrinks as the output voltage grows.
g_m = I_C/(kT/q) is the slope of the exponential at the bias current.
The Early voltage sets r_o = V_A/I_C.
Same controlled source and r_o; the new part is r_π, because the base draws current.
